articles.title: Solo diners are asking restaurants for half-size portions, sparking debate over menu flexibility
articles.summary: Solo dining is up 22% year over year, and some chefs will happily make half orders so diners alone can try more dishes without wasting food.
articles.body: As solo dining continues to surge in popularity, there is debate over whether it’s acceptable for guests dining alone at a restaurant to request a smaller portion size of a dish. Reservations for one saw a 22% increase year over year in the third quarter of 2025, according to a report from restaurant technology company Toast. One appealing part of dining out with a group is sharing plates and trying bites of many different dishes. RESTAURANTS DRAW THE LINE ON SUBSTITUTIONS AS DINERS PUSH MENU LIMITS Solo diners who still want to sample a variety of items without having an overwhelming amount of food on their table may be able to do so by simply asking their server if they can place a half-order, Food & Wine reported. Opinions are divided online about whether this is an acceptable request, with some believing that it’s no big deal while others say it’s not worth it. "Don't even bother, order the regular meal. And when it comes, you eat what you want of it, and anything that you have left over, get a to go box and take it home," one person wrote on Quora. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Many restaurants don’t appreciate when an adult orders a smaller portion size, the commenter added, saying, "they consider it to be a waste of their cooking time to make small portions for an adult." Plus, they noted, it doesn't hurt to have leftovers. Some chefs are happy to serve smaller portions to a solo diner because they want them to have a positive dining experience and be able to try many different dishes without wasting as much food, Food & Wine noted. "It never hurts to ask!" another Quora user said, with the caveat that certain dishes are more easily re-portioned than others. "Whether or not you are successful in your request depends on a few things. If the dish is pre-proportioned, then it’s not likely," they noted. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS For example, if an entree contains a half lobster tail, it’s probably not likely that the kitchen will scale that component down, the commenter continued, adding that restaurants may refuse to serve whole fishes and meats, portioned desserts or pizzas in smaller sizes. The important thing for diners to remember, they said, is that they will probably pay full price for a dish even if it’s a half-sized portion, because it takes an equal amount of time and effort to make. One Reddit user agreed that the portion sizes of certain dishes are more easily adjusted than others. "I think it’s easier with pasta dishes because they can portion out the amount of pasta, sauce, garnish, etc and keep selling the rest. Not so easy with a piece of protein (1/2 steak, 1/2 fish filet, 1/2 burger) because those are generally pre-portioned for service," they said. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Another person noted that they wanted a smaller portion to reduce food waste — and a smaller bill would be nice, too. "I hate wasting food, but if I eat the full portion I’m overeating and will feel sick. I’d love to do a half portion for a slightly cheaper price and not overeat or waste food," they said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP One Redditor shared that they were pleasantly surprised when a restaurant they dined solo at charged them half of the menu price for a half-sized portion.

articles.title: Netanyahu’s Likud, Eisenkot’s Yashar end coalition talks without deal
articles.summary: Parties remain split over who will lead the next government and whether far-right minister Itamar Ben-Gvir will join.
articles.body:
Talks between the parties of caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot to form a unity government have ended without a deal.

Representatives of Netanyahu’s Likud and Eisenkot’s Yashar parties met in a Herzliya hotel on Sunday, where they remained split on who would lead the next government and whether far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir would be part of it, according to Israel’s Channel 12 broadcaster.

The Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper reported that Likud wanted Ben-Gvir in government, while Yashar insisted on his exclusion.

In a joint statement, the two parties said they had “outlined their positions on a range of substantive issues” and that a “follow-up meeting would be held”, without revealing a date or any further details.

Eisenkot has until December 6 to form a government, with the possibility of a 14-day extension, after the elections in October gave his bloc 48 seats – 13 short of a majority.

Netanyahu has called for a unity government , saying it was the only way that Israel’s security could be guaranteed. Such an arrangement would allow a government to be formed without the inclusion of parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel, which won a record 19 seats.

Channel 12 reported that former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, who leads the Together list, proposed a coalition of Together, Yashar, Likud and Avigdor Lieberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu, with Eisenkot serving first and Netanyahu succeeding him.

However, Eisenkot has opposed a rotation, and Netanyahu has reportedly insisted on taking the premiership first, while Lieberman has ruled out joining any government that includes Netanyahu altogether.

If unity talks fail, Yashar plans to seek a confidence vote in the Knesset for a minority government before Eisenkot’s mandate expires. It would rely on outside support from the Arab Joint List, led by Yousef Jabareen, and the United Arab List, led by Mansour Abbas.

images.caption: An election billboard in Tel Aviv shows caretaker Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, left, and leader of the Yashar party, Gadi Eisenkot [File: Abir Sultan/EPA]

articles.title: Russian ship docked in Libya hit in suspected drone attack
articles.summary: A Russian ship docked at a naval base in Benghazi was severely damaged in a suspected Ukrainian drone attack Sunday, according to Libyan officials. The Merkury, a Russian navy corvette, was struck by two sea drones while docked in the eastern Libyan port city, triggering an explosion and a fire. An initial investigation found that…
articles.body:
A Russian ship docked at a naval base in Benghazi was severely damaged in a suspected Ukrainian drone attack Sunday, according to Libyan officials.

The Merkury, a Russian navy corvette, was struck by two sea drones while docked in the eastern Libyan port city, triggering an explosion and a fire. An initial investigation found that several drones were launched from a base operated by Ukrainian forces in western Libya, the officials told The Associated Press. Ukraine has not claimed responsibility for the attack.

At least four drones were intercepted and destroyed before two struck the warship. Libya’s eastern-based government said the vessel had stopped in Benghazi to refuel and resupply before returning to Russia under a maritime cooperation agreement between the two countries.

Officials said it had launched a joint investigation with Russia to determine who was responsible for the suspected attack. Russia has maintained close ties with authorities in eastern Libya, using Benghazi as a logistical hub for its military operations in Africa and its presence in the Mediterranean.

The strike comes amid a series of attacks against Russian vessels during its nearly five-year war in Ukraine.

On Saturday, a Russian cargo ship, the Sparta II, was struck by drones in the Baltic Sea, sparking a fire that continued into Sunday. Finland’s military said Ukraine was likely responsible for the attack, which occurred in international waters near Russia’s Gogland island.

All 16 crew members were evacuated to a nearby Russian vessel, with one person suffering minor injuries.

Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo warned that the fighting between Russia and Ukraine was reaching dangerously close to Finland’s borders.

“War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity,” Orpo wrote Saturday on the social platform X, translated from Finnish to English by the AI tool Grok. “The Finnish authorities are handling the situation in the Gulf of Finland, where a drone strike has hit a Russian merchant vessel. Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor.”

articles.title: Abdul El-Sayed suggests Israel should not be a Jewish state, says he opposes ‘ethno-states’
articles.summary: Michigan Democratic Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed suggested that Israel must choose between being a Jewish state and a democracy, urging equal rights above all else.
articles.body: Michigan Democratic Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed questioned whether Israel can maintain its identity as a Jewish state while upholding democratic principles, reiterating his opposition to "ethno-states." El-Sayed argued that Israel, founded as a Jewish nation in 1948, should prioritize democracy and equal rights for all its citizens during an interview on NBC’s "Meet the Press" on Sunday. "I don’t believe in ethno-states," he told host Kristen Welker. "I believe in equal rights to peace, dignity and self-determination." MICHIGAN SENATE CANDIDATE CONFRONTED REPEATEDLY OVER ISRAEL’S RIGHT TO EXIST, DEFUNDING THE POLICE "We’ve been told for a very long time that Israel is a Jewish democratic state, and I think folks are having to choose, is it a Jewish state or a democratic state?" he added. "And I would argue based on our principles that we should always be putting democracy over everything else." El-Sayed said it is "not a far stretch" to ask Israel to employ a democracy more strongly aligned with the U.S. and allow for equal rights, including religion, to be upheld. ACTOR MANDY PATINKIN URGES JEWISH VOTERS TO SUPPORT ABDUL EL-SAYED FOR THEIR OWN 'SAFETY' "We dignify the fact that, you know, though our skin color might be different, though we may pray different ways, that America and American laws respect us all the same," the Michigan Democrat said. "The idea that any government that we are supporting ought to uphold those very basic, same ideals is not a far stretch." "I just think it’s important for us to be clear about the principles of democracy, the principles of justice, and the principles of equal rights to peace, dignity, and self-determination for Palestinians and Jewish Israelis alike," he added. ABDUL EL-SAYED HITS BACK AT ISRAEL QUESTIONS, SUGGESTS HIS NAME AND FAITH ARE BEHIND PRESS SCRUTINY Welker noted that 43 countries currently identify with a particular religion, including Pakistan which is an Islamic republic and Denmark, a constitutionally Christian country. She asked El-Sayed why he believes Israel should abandon its national identity. "Well, I don’t believe in ethno-states generally," he responded. "I don’t think we should be in the business of funding the military of Pakistan either. I’m just trying to apply my ideals evenly." Fox News Digital reached out to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for comment. 'THE VIEW' CO-HOST CONFRONTS ABDUL EL-SAYED ON HIS RESPONSE TO ATTACK ON JEWISH SYNAGOGUE In a comment to Fox News Digital, Rabbi Yaakov Menken, executive vice president of the Coalition for Jewish Values, criticized El-Sayed for repeatedly singling out Israel despite exemplifying the democratic values he admires. "El-Sayed claims that he doesn't believe in ‘ethnostates,’ but only attacks the one country in the Middle East that provides the equal rights to peace, dignity, and self-determination that he claims to support," Menken said. "He conveniently forgets that 77% of Palestine is today's Jordan — which receives billions of dollars of U.S. aid, has been entirely ethnically cleansed of Jews since 1948, and which maintains racist laws even today that exclude Jews from regaining citizenship there." El-Sayed suggested last week that some concerns surrounding his so-called "antisemitism" reflect "discomfort" rather than a threat to safety. "If it is your sense of your discomfort and/or fear of safety that has to keep me quiet while I watch 70,000 people get killed, their homes annihilated, their hospitals destroyed, their universities decimated, and I can't critique that, then I think what you're telling me is that their humanity matters less than yours, and I'm not going to be OK with that," he told The Atlantic. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP El-Sayed, who has been a vocal supporter of the Free Palestine movement, criticized Israel's policies toward Palestinians, arguing that generations of Palestinian families have been denied the opportunity to establish their own state. "I just think it's important to remember that there are also Palestinian people whose families have been in the Holy Land for generations and those folks have been told that they are going to have a state of their own only to watch as the Israeli state is expanding, and we are supporting it," he told NBC.

articles.title: Trump to host private dinner for largest owners of his meme coin
articles.summary: Sunday’s dinner is the third event for top holders of the $Trump meme coin, launched shortly before his inauguration.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump will host a third private dinner for top investors in his meme coin $TRUMP, reigniting questions about potential conflicts of interest with his cryptocurrency ventures.

Sunday’s gala will take place at the Trump National Golf Club outside Washington, DC.

According to the dinner’s official website, the top 185 meme-coin holders will be invited to a gala dinner, where guests will include businessman Kevin O’Leary and boxer Floyd Mayweather.

The top 29 holders, meanwhile, will be given special access to a VIP reception where Trump will reportedly be present.

“There will be no private meetings with The President. No gifts will be accepted,” the website said of the VIP reception.

The event has been billed as “a once-in-a-lifetime experience — an evening you will talk about forever”.

But Democrats have accused the Republican leader of leveraging his public office for profit in violation of federal law. They see such dinners as an opportunity for private interests to pay for access to the president.

“Trump is continuing to exploit the presidency for his personal gain,” Kendall Witmer, the deputy communications director for the Democratic National Committee, said in a statement.

In October, shortly after the gala was announced, eight Democratic senators issued an open letter promising to investigate any conflicts of interest such an event might raise.

“President Trump’s continued monetization of his name and likeness once again raises serious ethical concerns, necessitating this request for a robust inquiry into the President’s financial entanglements and personal profiteering,” the letter said.

The Democratic Party has since won majorities in both chambers of Congress in the November 3 midterm race, paving the way for possible inquiries and subpoenas when the new members are sworn in next year.

Trump’s White House has dismissed the criticism, calling the dinner a “private event, not a government function”. It has also emphasised that “there is no promise of official government action in exchange for attending”.

Trump has also argued that many of his assets are held in a trust while he is in office, though that trust is largely run by his family members.

The president is a stakeholder in cryptocurrency firms like World Liberty Financial, and has made promoting cryptocurrency a central part of his second term.

Under his leadership, the US Treasury established a reserve of digital currency assets, as part of Trump’s effort to make the US the “crypto capital of the world”.

Sunday’s gala is believed to be the third such dinner for top $Trump meme coin holders.

Meme coins trade on a popular likeness from the internet. Trump launched his on January 17, 2025, days before the start of his second term.

To encourage meme-coin purchases, Trump and his business partners held private events on May 22, 2025, and again on April 25, 2026, for top holders of the cryptocurrency.

The first was held at the same Trump golf club outside Washington, DC, and the second took place at Mar-a-Lago, Trump’s Florida resort.

The May 2025 dinner reportedly required a minimum of $55,000 in $Trump coins to attend.

At the time, Chinese crypto investor Justin Sun was declared the winner of a “contest” for who held the most $TRUMP coins. Sun held about $18m of the coin in 2025, as well as tokens from World Liberty Financial.

Earlier this year, Sun sued World Liberty Financial , saying it had frozen his access to the assets he owned with it, making it impossible for him to sell them.

Trump’s inauguration in January 2025 proved a major boost for his coin, pushing its value to $74.

The $Trump coin has since lost value. On the eve of the gala dinner, it is worth about $0.88.

According to financial disclosure forms released earlier this year, Trump earned more than $2.2bn in 2025, the first year of his second term.

Much of that wealth came from meme coins, tokens and other digital assets. Some $636m came from $Trump meme coin sales.

articles.title: Burnham to tell MPs 'landmark' EU deal could make next decade 'much better'
articles.summary: The prime minister will tell MPs the deal agreed on Friday is a "choice between a broken status quo or change".
articles.body:
The prime minister will tell Parliament on Monday the "landmark" deal struck with the EU means there is a "very real prospect" the next decade can be "much better" than the last one.

The deal is a "choice between a broken status quo or change", Andy Burnham will tell MPs.

He will also call it "the single biggest growth measure to be delivered in this parliament" - repeating his claim it could add £17bn to the British economy.

The PM described it on Friday as a "win-win" deal with the EU on British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme. But since then a host of politicians have criticised the plan, with one former prime minister urging him to "move on" from Brexit.

Burnham believes the agreement reached in Brussels "holds out the very real prospect that the next decade can be a much better one for Britain than the one we have just lived through".

"The ability to draw a line on a decade of drift and division is in our hands and I believe we should take it," he will say in his speech.

He will also paint the move as a choice "between easing pressure on the cost of living or allowing food prices to rise further" and "creating opportunities for young people or denying them".

He believes polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".

But his announcement on Friday was greeted with a chorus of criticism from a number of opposing political figures.

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal was unfair because UK farmers would now have to follow rules made by Brussels.

She questioned the Treasury's analysis, which Burnham said suggested the deal "will add up to 0.5%" to UK gross domestic product and he described it as a "£17bn boost to the British economy".

Badenoch accused him of having "plucked that figure out of the air" before saying "the only modelling I've seen that even talks about that figure says it's actually 0.0%".

Meanwhile Reform UK leader Farage called the deal a "very good day for the EU", before adding: "A good day to try and humiliate the one member state that actually had the courage to say, 'We don't need to be part of you, we can govern our own country'."

Farage, who was a leading figure in the 2016 campaign to get Britain out of the EU, added in a social media post: "Like every prime minister before him, Burnham is a total fraud. Only Reform will stop the endless betrayal of the British people."

Over the weekend former prime ministers including Theresa May, Sir Tony Blair and Rishi Sunak also criticised the EU-UK deal.

May, who presided over three years of Brexit negotiations during her premiership, said she was "aghast" by the deal and warned Andy Burnham should "move on".

Sir Tony, who was a prominent opponent of leaving the EU, told The Sunday Times Britain should only rejoin the EU if it reforms, and allows more innovation on technology.

Badenoch will use her speech at the Confederation of British Industry (CBI) annual conference on Monday to criticise Burnham's EU deal.

She will accuse the prime minister of securing a "terrible" deal and will say he should be "aiming a lot higher" in terms of driving growth.

Farage will tell the same conference that establishing closer ties with the EU would be a "disaster" for British businesses.

Rejoining the EU will hit the small firms that do not even trade with Europe with more red tape, more compliance costs, more Brussels rules they never asked for, he is expected to say.

On Friday, the PM said that over the coming months both sides will "seek to conduct an informal brainstorming process" to look at the options for the UK's "long-term relationship" with the EU.

He was also clear that the deal he struck was "probably the limit of what we can achieve in this Parliament, given what needs to be done to implement it".

He added: "But we want to inform the Parliament after this one, so that decisions can be taken about that long-term relationship."

articles.summary: Democrat Chuck Hubbard has defeated GOP Rep. Virginia Foxx for a congressional seat in North Carolina, NBC News projects, adding to a Democratic wave that is projected to deliver the party at least 258 House seats.
articles.body: Democrat Chuck Hubbard has defeated GOP Rep. Virginia Foxx for a congressional seat in North Carolina, NBC News projects, adding to a Democratic wave that is projected to deliver the party at least 258 House seats. It’s the largest House majority that any party has held this century, according to the Office of the House Historian. It’s also the largest Democratic majority since 1992, when the party also won 258 seats. The party cemented control of the chamber not only by winning competitive races in battleground districts, but also by winning in deeply Republican areas that voted for President Donald Trump by double-digit margins just two years ago. In 2024, Trump won Foxx’s district by almost 18 percentage points, per an NBC News Decision Desk analysis. See the live U.S. House election results here, with four races still to be called. COP31 climate talks break down after angry dispute over fossil fuels International climate talks in Turkey broke down Sunday after the European Union and other nations rejected a draft agreement that had cut all references to fossil fuels. Negotiations fell apart two days after the United Nations’ COP31 conference was meant to end, after delegates from 196 countries and the European Union struggled to agree on new pledges for climate action and how to deliver on previous promises. COP31 President Murat Kurum said Sunday that there would be no new climate agreement draft after a fourth draft was rejected. “There is nothing to do. We did all that we could,” said Kurum, who is host nation Turkey’s environment minister. “​We will not ​be carrying out ​work on a new ⁠text in an environment ⁠where there ​is no consensus.” ‘Meet the Press’ Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich., said Sunday that he’s open to working with President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance to bring down costs and improve healthcare for Americans. Asked whether he intended to meet with the president or vice president soon, El-Sayed told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” that “plans are in the works.” One of the key proposals from the senator-elect’s campaign was to pass a measure that would guarantee healthcare for all Americans. On Saturday, he engaged with Trump on social media with a post on X suggesting that new healthcare legislation could be named “Trumpcare.” “Donald, this is on the table. Guarantee healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave,” El-Sayed wrote, alongside images of a gold health insurance card with “Trumpcare” inscribed on it. Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., said on “Meet the Press” Sunday that “momentum is in our direction” in his bid for Senate majority leader. Asked whether he believes he can secure enough votes to oust current party leader Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., Van Hollen said yes. “Yes, because if you look at our caucus, you can see a huge appetite for change,” he said. “They are seeing the American people and the Democratic Party calling for change. They also want to change the way we do business in the United States Democratic caucus and the United States Senate.” Politics in brief Coordinated response: Trump ordered federal contractors to check with White House before responding to inquiries from Congress. Thanksgiving travel off to a rough start with Delta delays and storms on the way A problem with the system Delta Air Lines uses to calculate aircraft weight and balance delayed its flights nationwide Sunday as Thanksgiving travel got underway. The Federal Aviation Administration lifted its ground delay program for Atlanta-bound Delta flights at 11:26 a.m. ET, but by 1:55 p.m. ET, 997 flights into and out of Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport had been delayed and 26 had been canceled, according to FlightAware. Delta said it was working to restore the automated system that calculates how much a plane weighs and how that weight is distributed before takeoff. The airline said it was coordinating with air traffic controllers to prevent congestion at gates and on the tarmac in Atlanta. Meanwhile, California officials this weekend are preparing for storms that could coincide with the year’s highest tides, Thanksgiving and some of its busiest holiday travel days. A Pacific storm expected to strike the Northern California coast Tuesday and Wednesday will bring with it an atmospheric river of rain, forecasters said. Rainfall of up to 3 inches is anticipated in parts of the San Francisco Bay Area, and a second storm was expected to swing behind the first. The first of the week’s storms also coincides with king tides, the highest of the year, which could result in serious flooding. Resources, including water rescue teams, are being mobilized across the state. Kansas City Current win first NWSL championship, defeating Washington Spirit Vanessa DiBernardo scored directly off a corner kick in the 54th minute to lift the Kansas City Current to their first championship in the National Women’s Soccer League, 2-1 over the Washington Spirit on Saturday night. articles.title: Army plans to invoke emergency provisions to detonate bomb-making chemicals in Iowa
articles.summary: The U.S.
articles.body: The U.S. Army plans to invoke emergency provisions to avoid a court order that had put on hold plans to detonate several tons of bomb-making chemicals in Iowa, saying that continued delays will make it more dangerous as the weather starts to turn colder. “To protect its personnel and the surrounding communities, the Army needs to take swift action,” government lawyers told the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in a filing late Saturday. “Protection of human health and the environment demand action now, not delay.” The Army plans to detonate the chemicals by Tuesday. Environmental groups criticized the government’s move, decrying it as a maneuver to get around a court order and avoid public demands for safety and transparency. The appeals court on Thursday granted a request by environmentalists to put on hold a permit that cleared the way for the detonation in Middletown, a small community about 160 miles southeast of Des Moines. It was initially planned for Friday, but the Army later announced that it would push the operation to Monday following an outpouring of public concern about potential health and environmental effects. Environmentalists have called for a review of the emergency permit that was approved earlier this month by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. In a statement Sunday, the Iowa Environmental Council, Sierra Club, and Earthjustice questioned claims that all alternatives were given appropriate consideration. “The Army seemed more concerned over the weekend with finding a way to sidestep the judicial process than on meeting the public’s demands for greater transparency, notice to affected communities, and far stronger protection of people, property, and the environment from serious harm,” said Earthjustice Attorney Thien Chau. Government lawyers said the Army doesn’t need a permit to take emergency action against an immediate threat from explosive material. They said the standards of a federal law regulating hazardous waste don’t apply in situations when there’s an immediate threat to health, safety or the environment as determined by an explosive or munitions emergency response specialist. Officials contend that the chemicals are unstable, and the risk of an uncontrolled explosion is growing, particularly as temperatures drop. They said there is a risk that the chemicals may explode as temperatures are expected to drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit in the coming days. In March, staff at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant found several dozen barrels of degraded lead azide, which is used in munitions production. Crystallization of the material created an unstable and dangerous situation, prompting the Army to assemble experts in munitions chemistry, engineering and environmental safety to come up with a plan. According to EPA documents, alternatives such as neutralizing and decomposing the drums’ contents with other chemicals were considered. But officials said handling the drums would increase the probability of an accidental, fatal detonation. The environmental groups disagreed, arguing in their petition that other alternatives were not fully considered. They also criticized officials for not sharing more information with the public. The Army had shared details during a public meeting in Middletown in October, but a public advisory a week ago was the first time other communities — some as far away as 100 miles — became aware of the potential impact. Nearly 400 people live in Middletown but thousands more in surrounding areas could be affected by detonated material that could disperse in the air and land on the ground. Vibrations from the two planned blasts were expected to be quick, but they could break old windows. That led officials to recommend some residents in Middletown vacate the area. Iowans in the region were told to stay inside; keep windows and doors closed; bring pets and livestock indoors; and clean cars, windowsills and outdoor surfaces afterward. “The detonation will result in an air plume with some lead-containing particles which will disperse in the air and deposit on the ground,” an advisory states. “Lead is toxic to humans and animals.”

articles.title: Molly Meldrum: Australian music legend dies aged 83
articles.summary: The promoter and broadcaster helped define the music tastes of Australians for decades.
articles.body:
Australian music industry legend Molly Meldrum has died aged 83 after a long illness.

The music promoter and broadcaster, born Ian Alexander Meldrum, helped define the nation's music tastes for decades, championing local artists like INXS and Kylie Minogue and global acts like Abba.

Known for his chaotic demeanour and trademark Stetson hat, he interviewed an array of stars from King Charles to Elton John, who described Meldrum as the "single most important influence in Australian pop music".

In a statement, Meldrum's family said he "passed away peacefully" at a hospital in Melbourne in the early hours of Monday morning.

"Affectionately dubbed 'the Guru', Molly was the heartbeat, the champion and the spirit of Australian music," the statement said.

Meldrum lived with an acquired brain injury after falling from a ladder in 2011.

Born in Victoria in 1943, he displayed a love of music from an early age and went on to host the Australian Broadcasting Corporation's music television programme Countdown, and later a segment on variety show Hey Hey, It's Saturday.

Meldrum in 2014 became the first person who was not a recording artist to be inducted into the Australian Recording Industry Association (Aria) Hall of Fame.

Among his most famous interviews was a 1977 sit-down with King Charles, in which Meldrum could not calm his jitters.

He stumbled over his lines, declaring: "Your Royal Highness... Oh, oh, I'm sweating like a pig".

King Charles reflected on the infamous interview for Countdown's 40th anniversary special , saying: "There is an old showbusiness saying which warns never to work with animals or children. But nobody prepared me for Molly Meldrum".

On Monday, Arts Minister Tony Burke said the country had lost an icon.

"One of his greatest legacies will be the generations of Australians who grew up with his unmistakable enthusiasm and love of music. A true champion of Australian talent, you will be missed, but never forgotten."

articles.title: Cameroon’s ex-rebels caught between hiding and broken promises
articles.summary: Cameroon’s former rebels face arrest fears and failed reintegration.
articles.body:
Douala, Cameroon – Collins Mbah says he hunted down and killed several Cameroonian soldiers in the English-speaking Northwest region during his time as a separatist fighter between 2016 and 2020. Today, in the coastal city of Douala, the man in his mid-30s, who went by the name Commander No Sorrow, has taken on a different role: traditional healer, tending to lives rather than taking them.

Mbah says he abandoned the armed struggle after realising that fellow fighters were turning against the very people they had set out to protect. But he has firmly ruled out joining the government’s disarmament, demobilisation and reintegration (DDR) programme.

“Quitting the struggle and joining the government disarmament programme would have meant I betrayed the people,” said Mbah, who dropped out of secondary school to join the revolt. “I don’t want to have anything to do with the government or the struggle any more. All I need now is peace of mind,” he told Al Jazeera.

October marked a decade since protests erupted in Cameroon’s English-speaking Northwest and Southwest regions, eventually escalating into an armed conflict between separatist fighters and government forces.

The unrest began in late 2016 after Anglophone lawyers and teachers protested against the appointment of Francophone magistrates unfamiliar with British common law to courts in English-speaking regions, and French-speaking teachers unable to communicate fluently in English to schools there. The protests were met with a government crackdown and eventually gave rise to a separatist movement seeking independence for the two regions, which its supporters call “Ambazonia”.

The conflict has killed thousands of people, displaced hundreds of thousands and disrupted education across the two English-speaking regions, according to humanitarian and human rights organisations. New figures released in October by the Cameroonian nonprofit Centre for Human Rights and Democracy in Africa (CHRDA) suggest the death toll could be as high as 10,000.

The fighting remains deadlocked, with separatist groups continuing attacks and kidnappings while the government pursues a military campaign. Alongside its military operations, the government has launched a community dialogue initiative, after distancing itself from Swiss- and Canadian-supported peace efforts.

Prime Minister Joseph Dion Ngute launched the initiative in Buea, the capital of Southwest, in September and in Bamenda, the capital of the Northwest, on October 15. Local leaders are being encouraged to persuade fighters to surrender and enter DDR centres. At the two events, 55 fighters – 25 in the Southwest and 30 in the Northwest – were presented as having renounced the armed struggle.

Despite leaving the rebellion, Mbah says he remains on the government’s wanted list. Without a national identity card, the father of three struggles to move freely around Douala and occasionally ventures into the outskirts to collect traditional herbs.

“I was initiated into traditional healing during childhood. The amulets and concoctions helped me foresee any danger when I was on the war front. Today, I use the same to heal,” he said. “But I don’t stay in a particular neighbourhood for long – I always move to the next to avoid being caught.”

Mbah is among former fighters who have chosen to reintegrate into society independently rather than enter government-run rehabilitation centres. Many say they fear arrest or poor treatment if they surrender.

Peter Mosongo, 28, now works as a motorcycle taxi rider in Buea after leaving the struggle in 2019. He joined in 2018 to protect his family but quit after witnessing what he describes as the indiscriminate killing of civilians by fellow fighters.

“I received threats from the fighters when I quit. They even kidnapped my father to force him to produce me,” Mosongo said. “I didn’t join DDR upon quitting out of fear that I may end up in prison. It was also being rumoured that those who surrendered were being killed silently.”

Mosongo says he also lost two cousins to the conflict.

Another former fighter, Richard Bende, left in 2019 because he believed the rebellion had become a “scores-settling venture”. He had fought government soldiers in Bamusso, in the Southwest, and now works as a secondary school history and geography teacher. Like Mbah and Mosongo, he avoided the DDR programme, citing concerns about the treatment of former fighters at its centres.

Paul Mukete, who fought in Kumba from 2017 to 2020 under the nickname King of Vultures, chose a different path. But six years after entering the DDR programme in Tiko town, in the Southwest, he says he has little to show for it.

Apart from learning poultry and pig farming, Mukete says he has received no psychological care.

“We gave intelligence information to the military, who used it to kill some separatist fighters who refused to lay down their weapons,” he said. “We were about 600 in the DDR centre, but many have since left out of frustration. Some even rejoined the struggle and got killed.”

The 29-year-old father of three now takes on odd jobs to support his family.

His account raises questions about whether the programme is providing former fighters with the support they need to rebuild their lives and remain out of the conflict.

Fonbeh Hedwick Chia, a mental health specialist and founder of the Bamenda-based Living Vine Mental Health Services, says both fighters and civilians in the English-speaking regions have been exposed to psychological trauma.

He argues that the DDR centres lack the therapeutic support needed to rehabilitate former fighters, estimating that about 800 have renounced the armed struggle.

“The government is more concerned with the propaganda made when they come to the DDR than their integral welfare,” Chia told Al Jazeera, arguing that former fighters need psychological care to address the trauma of atrocities committed and witnessed during the conflict.

Without proper rehabilitation, he warns, former fighters risk remaining marginalised and could become a source of further instability.

The accounts of former fighters and Chia’s assessment point to a central challenge for the DDR programme: persuading rebels to surrender is only the first step, while helping them return to civilian life requires sustained support.

Cameroon’s Anglophone crisis has roots in its colonial past. Initially colonised by Germany in 1884, the territory was divided between Britain and France after World War I.

French Cameroon gained independence in 1960. In 1961, British-administered Southern Cameroons voted in a United Nations-organised plebiscite to join the independent Republic of Cameroon, forming a federal state. The arrangement was dissolved in 1972 following a controversial referendum, ending the Anglophone regions’ federal status.

Unlike some conflicts involving more centralised rebel movements, Cameroon’s separatist rebellion has no single command structure. Dozens of smaller factions operate across Northwest and Southwest, with some receiving financial support and weapons from diaspora groups.

The prolonged fighting has brought human rights abuses by both government forces and separatists. Some armed groups have also shifted towards criminal activities, including kidnapping for ransom.

Chris Roberts, a political scientist at the University of Calgary in Canada, says the conflict is rooted less in language differences than in “decades of poor governance from a political system that has kept the same president in power since 1982”.

Although the government has repeatedly claimed the war is over, Roberts says continued firefights, ambushes and attacks demonstrate otherwise.

He argues that political reform in Yaoundé is essential to ending the conflict. He describes the October 2025 presidential election as “strategically rigged” and argues that it offers little prospect of resolving the crisis. A future presidential succession crisis could create opportunities for reform but also risk destabilising the country.

“There will not be a military solution to this war,” Roberts said.

articles.title: Urgent warning issued to cruise passengers about strict new law in Mexico
articles.summary: Cruise passengers visiting Mexico with minors need passports, birth certificates and notarized letters under a new law. The government passed the measure to combat child trafficking.
articles.body: Cruise passengers are being warned they may need to provide extensive documentation for onshore activities at ports in Mexico. The sweeping law now requires adults traveling to Mexico with minors to prove their relationship to the children in the group, or face denial of service at hotels, resorts and tours, the "Royal Caribbean Blog" reported. Effective Nov. 14, 2026, an amendment to Mexico's General Tourism Law places pressure on tourism providers to verify family relationships, according to Travel Market Report. CRUISE TIPPING CHARGES ARE 'OUT OF CONTROL' SAY PASSENGERS AS COMPANIES TOUT 'EXCEPTIONAL SERVICE' The Mexican Senate unanimously passed the measure to combat child trafficking and exploitation, aiming to shed the country's status as a major destination for such crimes. Fox News Digital reached out to Sen. Torres and Royal Caribbean for additional information. Travelers should be prepared to present passports, long-form birth certificates and custody or guardianship paperwork, the same blog noted. Documentation explaining any differing last names between a parent and child is also recommended. Even if cruise passengers are only stopping in a Mexican port for the day, the rules apply to all local services. 11-NIGHT CARIBBEAN CRUISE ABRUPTLY CANCELED AFTER COAST GUARD DETAINS SHIP While simply disembarking from a cruise ship might not trigger a document check, booking a beach club day pass, a local snorkeling excursion or renting a vacation home likely will, the blog reported (it is not affiliated with Royal Caribbean). Travelers are urged to call hotels and tour operators in advance to confirm paperwork requirements. Having both lost or stolen while out of the country would be very stressful to deal with." articles.title: Asian stock markets tumble as AI bubble fears mount
articles.summary: Stocks fall in South Korea, Taiwan and Hong Kong amid tech-led sell-off.
articles.body:
Asian stock markets have opened to sharp losses amid mounting concerns over the sustainability of the AI boom.

Key indexes in South Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong and mainland China fell on Monday, continuing Friday’s tech-led sell-off on both sides of the Pacific.

The Korea Composite Stock Price Index (Kospi) in Seoul slid as much as 4.5 percent in morning trading, while Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Index dipped 1.8 percent.

The CSI 300 Index in Shanghai dropped more than 1.3 percent, while the Taiwan Stock Exchange Capitalization Weighted Stock Index (Taiex) swung between losses and gains after falling more than 1 percent at opening.

Japan’s stock markets were closed for Labour Thanksgiving Day.

On Friday, Wall Street’s benchmark S&P 500 closed 3.7 percent lower for its seventh straight loss, while the tech-focused Nasdaq Composite dropped 5.3 percent to erase all of its gains for 2026, following a rout in Asia.

The Kospi, Nikkei 225, and the Taiex entered the weekend between 5.1 percent and 6.2 percent lower, while the Hang Seng Index finished down 1.9 percent.

Wall Street appeared on track for a rebound on Monday, with S&P 500 and Nasdaq futures up 2 percent and 2.4 percent, respectively.

Investors have long been concerned that tech firms may not be able to sustain the multi-trillion-dollar investments they have poured into the infrastructure needed to train and run AI.

Global AI-related investment, much of it fuelled by debt, is expected to reach $2.7 trillion in 2026 and $3.6 trillion in 2027, according to technology insights company Gartner.

Concerns that the AI boom may be running out of steam have been exacerbated by growing calls for greater oversight of the sector.

The Democratic Party’s sweeping victory in the US midterm elections is expected to slow data centre construction in US states, while the alleged espionage scandal embroiling chip giant Nvidia and its former CEO Jensen Huang has led to a push for tighter restrictions on China’s access to advanced chips.

articles.title: What is going on with Poundland?
articles.summary: Poundland has a matter of days to find a buyer or face collapsing into administration. Why?
articles.body:
The future of Poundland hangs in the balance as it faces a possible collapse into administration.

Its owner, US investment firm Gordon Brothers, put it up for sale in September, but then rejected offers to keep the business afloat.

Poundland has a major presence on the High Street, with 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, where it trades under the Dealz brand.

If it were to collapse, the jobs of its 11,000 employees would be at risk, as well as potentially thousands of others at firms that supply the retailer.

Have people stopped shopping at Poundland?

People have not stopped shopping at Poundland - quite the opposite.

Although the chain was struggling when it was sold by Pepco last year for £1, the business turned a corner over the year to September, going from a £68m loss to an £18.1m profit before interest, tax and certain accounting charges.

Going into the vital Christmas period, first-quarter like-for-like sales were up 7% and operational profits of £1.9m were up £1.2m on last year.

Halloween sales were 11.4% higher than last year - this is usually a good indicator of how a retailer will do at Christmas, says retail analyst Catherine Shuttleworth of Savvy Marketing.

According to Julie Palmer, managing partner at insolvency specialist Begbies Traynor: "This isn't a story about shoppers abandoning Poundland. The tills are busier than they were a year ago."

She adds: "On the face of it, a turnaround seems well under way."

However, Gordon Brothers has been restricting Poundland's access to cash needed to restock stores and meet day-to-day expenses.

It had frozen about £50m in funds leading to concerns Poundland's shops would run out of stock.

However, Gordon Brothers released around £21m over two weeks recently, giving the chain a little more breathing space.

Poundland seems to be facing "a funding and ownership problem rather than a trading collapse", Palmer says.

However, while Poundland boss Barry Williams says the business is making a "strong recovery", Gordon Brothers has painted a different picture, saying the chain remains "challenged and vulnerable to any potential downturn in future trading".

It says it has provided significant funding to support the company's ability to trade since it acquired the business.

It has also made about £18m from a combination of debt interest payments and other fees and charges.

As well as being Poundland's owner, it is one of its lenders, and is owed loans, including a £22.5m shareholder loan it inherited when it bought the business for £1.

As the main creditor, Gordon Brothers would be first in line to get paid back if the business goes under - but its suppliers are not.

"When the owner is also the main lender, its first priority is recovering [loans]," says Palmer. "Sometimes the route that best protects the lender is different from the one that saves the most jobs, and that tension is why this has become such a political story."

Irish firm Martin Property Group has offered to buy the business as a going concern, while London-based holding company Xyra Group has also made a rescue bid , although doubts remain about the credibility of Xyra's offer.

There is also a third, unnamed bid on the table.

Gordon Brothers has also been weighing options to break Poundland up.

The US company's view is that ultimately breaking the retailer up will provide more security for employees in the long term, because any buyers of its store estate will also have to agree to keep the employees on.

Insiders who are critical of how Gordon Brothers has handled the Poundland sale say it is driving the business into the ground to make money through the insolvency process.

But the investment firm, which specialises in buying and restructuring distressed companies, has denied the claim.

For now, Poundland has avoided immediate collapse after a deadline was extended by 10 days to find a rescue deal .

Shuttleworth says the future of Poundland is "really unclear, with the owners and the management at loggerheads about its future".

Palmer says there are two ways forward for Poundland - either a solvent deal, where the company gets bought and carries on trading, or a collapse followed by a break-up.

"The immediate make-or-break issue is Christmas: a value retailer that can't get stock on its shelves in November and December is in serious trouble, whatever its full-year results say," says Palmer.

There has been political pressure on Gordon Brothers from both Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds. They have called for answers over why the Martin Property Group offer to buy the business, which would have protected jobs, was rejected.

A committee of MPs also questioned Gordon Brothers last week, adding to pressure.

But Shuttleworth says that as a US firm Gordon Brothers appears "unmoved" by the arguments that the UK government has put forward.

articles.title: Mark Ruffalo doubles down on call to oust Schumer over 'entrenched religious beliefs and loyalties'
articles.summary: Actor Mark Ruffalo said Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., is too beholden to "entrenched religious beliefs" to lead, sparking bipartisan backlash from critics.
articles.body: Actor Mark Ruffalo said Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., was too beholden to "entrenched religious beliefs and loyalties" to lead the Senate in a post on X, advocating for Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., as Senate majority leader. "Israel is just one issue in a whole host of reasons Van Hollen is the right leader for our times. We need Justice, we need leadership that follows the will of the people not entrenched religious beliefs and loyalties," Ruffalo wrote on X. "Does not follow entrenched fossil fuel and corporate interests, nor throws a blind eye to the hard realties [sic] we face today." The four-time Academy Award nominee argued that Van Hollen had the integrity, strength and spirit to fight "the social and moral corruption that has set in with age-old presumptions" in the incoming Democratic-led Congress. BILL MAHER BLASTS DEMOCRATIC PARTY, SAYS IT IS FINE WITH RELIGION 'AS LONG AS THAT FAITH ISN’T JEWISH' "We have absolutely nothing to lose by replacing Sen. Schumer," Ruffalo wrote. "We can only gain more justice and freedom. Put pressure on your senators. Now is the time. Keep the momentum of this election going. Thank you, Senator Schumer, but it’s time to move aside." Ruffalo faced backlash across both sides of the political aisle for what critics viewed as a slight against Schumer's Jewish background. "Entrenched religious beliefs? Entrenched loyalties? Please elaborate, @MarkRuffalo," Anti-Defamation League CEO and National Director Jonathan Greenblatt wrote. "Which religion? Loyal to whom?" "There are many devout Senators & Congressmen with 'entrenched religious beliefs.' Chuck Schumer is not one of them," Rabbi Yaakov Menken, executive vice president of the Coalition for Jewish Values, wrote. "Van Hollen is far more tied to the Episcopal Bishop of Washington than Schumer is to any leading Rabbi. Guess what really bothers Ruffalo." RABBINIC GROUP ACCUSES JEWISH ENTERTAINERS OF 'WHITEWASHING ANTISEMITISM' IN MARK RUFFALO DEFENSE "Can you clarify what you mean by 'entrenched religious beliefs and loyalties'?" political commentator Meghan McCain asked. By Sunday, Ruffalo doubled down on his post, citing Schumer's 2018 comments at the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) annual policy conference where he was quoted saying, "Of course, we say it’s our land, the Torah says it, but they don’t believe in the Torah. So that’s the reason there is not peace." "These are Senator Schumer’s words, not mine," Ruffalo added on X. "Schumer is entitled to his religious beliefs, but those beliefs cannot determine the rights of another people. And they certainly cannot substitute for international law," Ruffalo continued. "This is a conflict about land, freedom, security, equality and self-determination. Peace requires justice, accountability and respect for the rights of both Palestinians and Israelis." Fox News Digital reached out to Ruffalo's representative and Schumer's office for comment. MORE THAN 180 JEWISH ENTERTAINERS RALLY BEHIND ACTOR MARK RUFFALO IN PROTEST LETTER Human rights attorney Brooke Goldstein, executive director of The Lawfare Project and Founder of the #EndJewHatred movement, denounced Ruffalo's posts, calling the actor "obsessively fixated" on the Jewish state to the point of questioning members of the party he supports. "And now they’re even turning on one of their own, Senator Chuck Schumer, because apparently even being a loyal Democrat isn’t enough when you’re Jewish," Goldstein told Fox News Digital. "They’re saying the quiet part out loud now, no longer afraid to invoke his Jewish identity as grounds for distrust. The message is unmistakable: ‘He’s a Jew. We can’t trust him.'" "His [Ruffalo's] obsessive fixation on the Jewish state, his selective outrage, and his breathtaking moral relativism raise serious questions about whether his "so called activism" is driven by genuine concern for America’s interests or by hostility toward Jews," she added. articles.title: WHO chief calls for peace amid heavy fighting in Ebola-hit DR Congo region
articles.summary: Fighting near a DRC hospital disrupts Ebola efforts, putting patients and workers at ‘grave risk’, WHO warns.
articles.body:
The World ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌Health Organization (WHO) chief has urged peace following heavy fighting in the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s (DRC) northeastern province, the epicentre of the Ebola outbreak.

WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠on ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠Sunday that fighting near a hospital in the DRC’s Ituri ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠province disrupted Ebola response efforts and forced health workers and aid partners to shelter ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠inside a maternity ward for more than 24 hours.

“Heavy fighting has been ongoing since yesterday in the vicinity of a hospital in Ituri – in an area close to where the Ebola outbreak first emerged,” Tedros said on X.

“The situation has disrupted the work of the hospital and the wider Ebola response, putting patients, families and health workers at grave risk.”

Medical staff have been sheltering for their lives in a maternity ward in the facility for more than 24 hours, and the WHO is working to arrange a safe exit for the team and “for the hospital facilities, staff and patients to be protected,” Tedros also said.

As of November 17, the WHO reported a total of 5,678 deaths out of 11,613 cases in the DRC, the largest and deadliest Ebola outbreak in the country.

The WHO said in a statement on Saturday that “while some areas had seen a slight decline in cases, sustained, high-level transmission continues overall in the country.”

Ituri and North Kivu, in the eastern part of the DRC, remain the most affected provinces.

The virus, which is transmitted through contact with bodily fluids, has spread across swaths of the DRC’s east and northeast, which have been plagued by violence for more than 30 years.

Earlier in November, armed men thought to be linked to an ISIL (ISIS)-affiliated group raided villages and killed dozens of people in North Kivu, forcing ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠patients with confirmed and suspected Ebola infections to flee.

The outbreak is also occurring amid ongoing fighting between government forces and the Rwanda-backed M23 armed group, which has seized key cities in eastern DRC, making transport of healthcare resources to remote regions difficult.

articles.title: Blended families: Holiday with your ex's kids and their mum?
articles.summary: Expert tips on how to get along with the mums and dads of your child's half-siblings.
articles.body:
When TV personality Laura Anderson announced she was going on holiday with her ex-partner's ex-wife Natasha Gray and their children, some friends were sceptical.

"They'd say to be wary of that relationship and not see it as genuine," she says.

While there is no formal title for the mums and dads of your child's half-siblings, Laura says she thinks of Natasha as her friend.

Laura, a radio host and former Love Island contestant, has a three-year-old daughter, Bonnie, with her ex, actor Gary Lucy.

Natasha, a nurse, was with Gary for 14 years prior to Laura's relationship with him and they have four children.

Laura tells CBeebies Parenting Download how she and Natasha built a friendship to enable their children to spend time with their half-siblings.

Also on the podcast, co-parenting expert Aaron Dale shares his experience of getting to know his son's stepfather and gives tips to other parents in a similar situation.

Laura was 14 when she found out she had a half-sister from her father's previous relationship and now the two are "very close".

She felt a responsibility to make sure her own daughter didn't "miss out on that sibling bond" and the idea of spending time with Natasha and her children developed naturally.

"Maybe there was a point that I wasn't fully ready when Bonnie was younger and I was still navigating my break-up," she says.

"But I became more comfortable with the idea and I thought, 'No, she's right. We need to make an effort'... It felt like a chance to give [Bonnie] more than just me and her."

Aaron - author of The Co-Parent: A Toolkit for Parenting Together, Apart - grew up on the same estate as his half-siblings but says his father never introduced them. His two sons have different mums.

"I made a promise to myself that my sons would never feel like they were 'half' anything. My sons are brothers, full stop."

Aaron co-parents with his ex-partners and says he has a "great relationship" with the stepdad to one of his sons. He says a blended family creates "a wider circle of love" for children.

"I've seen this first hand with my son's stepfather. Not only does he have an amazing relationship with my son, but so does his daughter and their wider family."

He acknowledges it's not always straightforward but says it's the responsibility of parents to "put differences aside".

"Whatever the dynamic looks like between the adults involved, your children's relationships with their siblings deserve to be a priority."

Aaron says it's important to take time to get to know the other adults in your child's family including their values, personality, interests and what they want from life.

"Don't become so consumed with how this person might fit into your child's world that you forget to consider whether they fit into yours," he says.

He advises having a conversation about the roles you would like each other to play, what you're comfortable with and where boundaries need to be established.

You should also respect "existing bonds", he adds. "You are becoming an extension of a child's existing family, not a replacement for somebody else.

"Don't enter a child's life feeling that you have to take somebody else's place, and don't make them feel that loving you somehow means being disloyal to another parent."

Laura's advice for getting to know your blended family is to "make it about the children".

"Be as selfless as possible and remove any negative feelings you might have towards your ex," she says.

Even if you initially feel rejected when trying to establish a blended family, she urges you not to "give up at the first hurdle".

Despite scepticism from friends, Laura says she and Natasha have proven their blended family works.

"I think they definitely changed their minds once they saw pictures of us all together. They'd say, "You look so comfortable and so happy.'"

Laura says the trip she had in the summer with Natasha and their children was "one of the best holidays" she had been on.

"I felt really comfortable and it was just love all round."

Laura and Natasha have booked a staycation in the Cotswolds to celebrate Christmas with their children.

"I've got matching PJs and someone's going to come in and cook for us - and we've got a Santa coming in."

She adds: "We want to have those memories, we just want to soak it all up."

articles.summary: DHAKA: Bangladesh Sunday appeared to soften its stand on the 1996 Ganga Water Sharing Treaty, shifting from its demand for a new agreement to hoping the
articles.body: DHAKA: Bangladesh Sunday appeared to soften its stand on the 1996 Ganga Water Sharing Treaty, shifting from its demand for a new agreement to hoping the political leadership in New Delhi will take steps to initiate formal negotiations for its renewal ahead of its expiry on Dec 12.India has maintained that the joint rivers commission is the established mechanism to discuss all water-related, cross-boundary river-related issues, including the Ganga treaty, even as Dhaka sought a fresh deal with a clause guaranteeing that its share of water during the dry season is protected and that New Delhi form a technical team to discuss the issue."We have already completed all necessary preparations related to the treaty," PM adviser on finance and planning Rashed Titumir, who also heads Bangladesh's 10-member technical committee on the treaty, told reporters. "We hope India will take effective measures to ensure the equitable and fair sharing of the waters of the international river Ganga," Titumir said.Bangladesh hopes that India will take the required steps before the expiry of the current term of the treaty to pave the way for the commencement of formal negotiations, he said, after the 91st meeting of the Bangladesh-India Joint Committee on the treaty's implementation in Dhaka.The four-member Indian delegation was led by India's Joint Rivers Commission chief Sharad Chandra while his counterpart Anwar Kadir led a six-member team. Titumir said, the two sides finalised the annual report on the implementation of the treaty for 2026.Sources, however, hinted that it is for the political leadership of the two countries to take a call on its renewal or interim extension and its terms, whatever the case may be. Bangladesh water resources minister Shahiduddin Chowdhury Anee recently sent a letter to his Indian counterpart through diplomatic channels to expedite discussions on the treaty, urging an early start to the negotiations.To initiate discussions, Bangladesh formed a high-level technical committee in June 2026 and informed India of the decision, requesting New Delhi to notify Dhaka about the formation of its own technical committee, he said. Bangladesh and India share 54 transboundary rivers, but the Ganga remains the only one covered by a bilateral water-sharing agreement between the two countries.You use AI every day. articles.title: Russian warship sinks off Libya as suspected Ukrainian strikes take war beyond Black Sea
articles.summary: The Russian corvette Merkury capsized at Benghazi Naval Base after suspected Ukrainian sea drones struck, injuring ten people, Libyan officials say.
articles.body: A Russian warship capsized and sank Sunday after suspected Ukrainian sea drones struck a naval base in eastern Libya, triggering an explosion and fire, according to Libyan officials. Hours later, a second drone attack also hit a commercial ship off the coast of Benghazi, Reuters reported. The first ship, the Russian navy corvette Merkury, was docked at Benghazi Naval Base when two explosive-laden sea drones struck the vessel, according to Libyan military officials who spoke to The Associated Press. UKRAINE POUNDS BLACK SEA FLEET’S ‘LAST MAJOR STRONGHOLD’ WHILE PUTIN FLEXES NAVAL POWER IN PACIFIC At least four other drones were intercepted and destroyed, the officials said. Satellite images showed most of the warship capsized and submerged, with only its bow remaining above water. Smoke could be seen rising from the ship's superstructure, and debris was scattered along the pier. Ten people, including Russian and Libyan nationals, suffered minor injuries in the attack and were receiving treatment in Benghazi, medical sources told Reuters. The warship had stopped at the port to refuel and resupply while returning to Russia under a maritime cooperation agreement with Libya's eastern-based government, officials said in a statement. Libyan military officials said an initial investigation indicated that Ukrainian sea drones had been launched from a base in western Libya, according to The AP. UKRAINE STRIKES DEEP INTO RUSSIA’S ARCTIC GAS HEARTLAND AS TRUMP PUSHES PUTIN TOWARD PEACE Hours after the warship was struck, a Maltese-flagged commercial ship was also hit by a sea drone off Benghazi, two Libyan military sources told Reuters. Libyan naval forces rescued the commercial ship's crew, while health officials reported that some crew members sustained minor injuries and were in stable condition. Libyan naval and air forces also intercepted more than 20 drone boats off Benghazi on Sunday evening, the military sources told Reuters. The attacks prompted Libya's eastern-based government to seek an international investigation. Prime Minister Osama Hamad said his government had submitted a formal request to the United Nations General Assembly and Security Council to investigate the attacks, including suspicions that the drones were launched from western Libya. RUSSIA DEPLOYS NORTH KOREAN MISSILE UNIT TO UKRAINE; MOSCOW-PYONGYANG AXIS DEEPENS: REPORT Hamad also called for an investigation into the possible presence of Ukrainian military experts in Libya and requested an explanation from Kyiv about their activities. The eastern government insisted that Libya was not a party to the war between Russia and Ukraine and condemned attempts to use its territory to settle foreign conflicts. "The Libyan government will not allow Libyan ports, territory or territorial waters to be turned into an arena for settling scores or exporting international conflicts," the government said. Benghazi is controlled by forces loyal to Gen. Khalifa Haftar, whose self-styled Libyan National Army dominates eastern and southern Libya and maintains close ties with Russia. Libya has been divided since the 2011 NATO-backed uprising that toppled longtime dictator Moammar Gadhafi. UKRAINE UNLEASHES MORE THAN 400 DRONES NEAR MOSCOW IN ONE OF WAR'S BIGGEST ATTACKS A U. N. recognized government operates from Tripoli, while a rival administration controls much of the east. The suspected attacks also come as Ukraine has expanded its campaign against Russian naval assets beyond the Black Sea. In December 2025, Ukraine said it struck a Russian-linked oil tanker with aerial drones in the Mediterranean Sea. In March 2026, Russia accused Ukraine of attacking a Russian liquefied natural gas tanker with naval drones launched from the Libyan coast. Libyan officials previously told the AP that Ukrainian drone specialists had been operating from military facilities in western Libya, including an air base in Misrata and sites in Tripoli and Zawiya. articles.title: 12-year-old Aaron Osirus borrowed $600 from his parents to buy a 3D printer and turned his playroom into a custom toy business with his twin brother
articles.summary: Aaron Osirus is 12 years old and already runs a business from his playroom.
articles.body: Aaron Osirus is 12 years old and already runs a business from his playroom. He noticed that many classmates carried fidget toys at school and decided to make his own. He borrowed $600 from his parents to buy a 3D printer with an automatic material system that can switch colours during printing, then began selling custom toys to classmates and neighbourhood kids. His twin brother, Alain, later joined him in running A3D. The twins earn about $200 in profit each month after paying for supplies and labour. Advanced Manufacturing gives the same monthly figure.How Aaron Osirus turned a $600 loan into a custom 3D-printed toy factoryAccording to CBS News, the idea came after Aaron noticed that many of his classmates carried fidget toys at school. He told the outlet he wondered why he could not make them himself, since they were all plastic: "If all these fidgets are plastic, why can't I make them?" Aaron noticed that a lot of his classmates were always playing with fidget spinners. That gave him the idea to make his own and sell them to other students, and A3D was born.Aaron borrowed $600 from his parents to buy a high-tech 3D printer. The machine has an automatic material system that can switch colours during the printing process.According to Advanced Manufacturing, the $600 loan from his parents paid for the 3D printer and the filament to make spinners and small toys. CBS News Atlanta reports that Aaron began by selling toys to classmates and neighbourhood kids. He customised each order to the customer's preferred design, size and colour, and then set a price and a delivery timeline.How twin brothers Aaron and Alain Osirus run their custom toy factoryAs demand grew, Aaron brought his twin brother, Alain Osirus, into the business. Alain says he is a designer for A3D, that he sometimes makes the toys and that he helps with marketing. He also checks how long each item takes, the cost and the fulfilment.The brothers produce popular items such as pass-through fidgets and articulated toys. Their most expensive product is a four-colour kitten that takes about a full day to print and sells for $5. Advanced Manufacturing says the brothers describe the kitten as their most popular item after fidget spinners and that it takes all day to print. Both outlets report that regular customers receive a 50-cent discount.$600 investment turned into a profitable toy business for two young brothersThe twins earn about $200 in profit each month after paying for supplies and labour. The outlet adds that, according to industry leaders PrintPal and SelfCAD, profit margins on 3D-printed products can range from 70% to 90% because the raw materials are relatively inexpensive. The brothers also keep costs down by asking friends whether they would like to volunteer before hiring additional help. The brothers figure they make about $200 in profit every month and rely on volunteers instead of employees.Aaron finds it rewarding to watch people play with his prints: "Oh yeah, that's really cool because I made it." CBS News Atlanta reports that the twins say the business has strengthened their bond and taught them lessons about investing, customer service and entrepreneurship. Aaron encourages other young people to follow their dreams and try their hardest, and says they need to save up the money and plan for everything. Alain also urges others to chase their dreams.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: India-Iran bilateral talks: Cultural cooperation, manuscript preservation, joint SCO heritage network discussed on sidelines of forum
articles.summary: India held bilateral talks with Iran on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Civilisational Dialogue Forum to explore avenues for
articles.body: India held bilateral talks with Iran on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Civilisational Dialogue Forum to explore avenues for cultural cooperation, with Tehran proposing the establishment of a joint network to preserve manuscripts and shared civilisational heritage.Union culture secretary Vivek Aggarwal confirmed the bilateral engagement on Sunday, saying the two countries remained in regular touch on areas of potential cultural exchange. He added that several ideas were discussed during the meeting, though no specific project had been finalised."There was a bilateral meeting with Iran. And India is in constant touch with Iran, and on areas in which there can be any cultural exchange, we are always in discussion. And discussions took place during the Summit too," Aggarwal told reporters at the historic Purana Quila, the venue of the three-day forum."Ideas have been thrown, though no such project has been concretised yet. But the discussions and engagements are on," he added.The Iranian Embassy in India, in a post on X on Sunday, said Tehran had proposed setting up an "SCO Joint Network for Written Heritage and Civilisational Memory" at the forum.Dr Faridoddin Faridasr, Cultural Counsellor of the Islamic Republic of Iran in India, addressed the First SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum in New Delhi, highlighting the importance of shared civilisational heritage as a foundation for cultural cooperation and mutual understanding among SCO member states, the embassy said.In his remarks, Faridasr emphasised the historical role of the Persian language as a language of science, literature, administration and cultural exchange across Central Asia, the Indian subcontinent and neighbouring regions, describing it as an important part of the shared cultural and historical heritage of the region.He also highlighted the work of the Noor International Microfilm Centre, affiliated with the Iranian Embassy in New Delhi, as an example of cultural cooperation between the two countries.Since 1990, the centre has collaborated with 72 academic and cultural institutions in India, resulting in the digitisation of "more than 150,000 Persian and Arabic manuscripts," the restoration and preservation of over three million pages of historical documents, and the preparation of nearly 300 catalogues, the embassy said.Faridasr also referred to ongoing joint projects with cultural institutions in Telangana and Hyderabad for the digitisation, restoration and preservation of historical Persian documents and manuscripts.Outlining the proposed SCO network as a practical initiative to strengthen regional cultural cooperation, the embassy said it would focus on preserving and digitising manuscripts and historical documents, exchanging technical expertise and providing training in manuscript restoration. It would also promote shared linguistic and literary heritage through joint research, publications and exhibitions.Faridasr reaffirmed Iran's "readiness to share its experience and technical expertise with other SCO member states", stressing that the preservation of shared civilisational heritage provided an opportunity to strengthen mutual trust, cultural understanding and cooperation across the region.Meanwhile, Aggarwal said no formal bilateral meeting took place between India and Pakistan on the sidelines of the forum, although members of the two sides interacted during banquets and conference sessions."There were no formal bilateral talks between the two sides," he said, responding to a question on whether any formal engagement had taken place between the two countries.He added that there were other "informal discussions" during the course of the event, including interactions with ministers and heads of delegations from participating countries."In general, there were also meetings between ministers and heads of delegations, as the aim of this (multilateral) forum is to exchange views, so there were many meetings, and a lot of things were discussed," the culture secretary said.Pakistan's Federal Minister Musadik Masood Malik, who attended the three-day forum, said he was in India to discuss regional issues and cultural ties in the context of the SCO, and not the Indus Waters Treaty."When you will call me for talk on Indus (Water Treaty), that time, we will surely talk on Indus (treaty). This time, you have not called me here for (talks on) the Indus treaty; this time you have called me to talk...," Malik told reporters."You have called me this time to talk about the issue in the context of the SCO forum, the regional issues, its relationship with culture, for which I am here," he said.The three-day forum, held from November 20 to 22, was organised by the Ministry of Culture and the Ministry of External Affairs. It was inaugurated by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on November 20 and saw the participation of delegates from various SCO member countries, including Iran and Pakistan, as well as other countries.Get the latest India News and Live updates.
