articles.summary: Purdue University professor Julie Tkach and her two teenage daughters died in an apparent murder-suicide in West Lafayette, Indiana, authorities say.
articles.body: This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or 1-800-273-TALK (8255). A Purdue University professor and her two teenage daughters were killed in an apparent murder-suicide last week after the father reportedly opened fire on his family before turning the gun on himself, according to Indiana authorities. Preliminary autopsy results identified the mother as Julie Tkach, 53, of West Lafayette, who died from multiple gunshot wounds, with her death ruled a homicide, the Tippecanoe County Coroner’s Office said Friday. Julie was a clinical assistant professor in Purdue University's Department of Hospitality and Tourism Management, according to her LinkedIn profile. The father, Thomas Tkach, 51, died by suicide from a gunshot wound to the head, officials said. He was employed by the Tippecanoe County Sheriff's Office as a courthouse security officer after previously serving as a jail deputy, according to local outlet Star City News., according to local outlet Star City News. KANSAS CONVICTED FELON, SEX OFFENDER ALLEGEDLY KILLS FELLOW FAMILY MEMBERS BEFORE TAKING HIS OWN LIFE: POLICE Their daughter, Katharyn, 17, died from multiple gunshot wounds to the head, while their other daughter, Lauren, 16, died from multiple gunshot wounds, the coroner's office said. West Lafayette Police said the family members were found inside their West Lafayette-area home Wednesday evening, Nov. 18, after officers responded to a 911 call shortly after 8:30 p.m. The coroner's office was subsequently notified of multiple deaths at roughly 1:50 a.m. Thursday. According to emergency dispatch audio obtained by Star City News, authorities received a separate concerning call shortly before the bodies were discovered. A dispatcher described receiving a call from one of the daughters. "She advised that her father had a gun and was threatening to shoot the family. I heard multiple gunshots go off and the line is now silent," the recording said. TWO TEEN SUSPECTS HELD AFTER 5 FAMILY MEMBERS KILLED IN 'TARGETED MASS SHOOTING' While officials have not disclosed a motive behind the killings, the coroner’s office urged anyone struggling with mental health challenges to seek help through available resources. Residents can call or text 988 to reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. Indiana State Police is leading the investigation because Thomas Tkach was employed by the Tippecanoe County Sheriff's Office. The West Lafayette Police Department described the incident as a "terrible night" that deeply affected its personnel, as well as those at the Tippecanoe County Sheriff's Office, which also responded to the scene. "Many people on my team and other teams have had a very difficult time with the incident that took place on Wednesday night," the sheriff’s office said. "The things seen and heard the other night will be remembered for the rest of their lives," the office added. DISPATCH AUDIO RELEASED IN MICHIGAN FAMILY MURDER-SUICIDE AS TROUBLED FAMILY'S SECRETS EMERGE According to LinkedIn, Julie had spent more than 20 years teaching and mentoring students in the hospitality industry. Prior to Purdue, she worked at South Dakota State University for eight years as a lecturer and instructor. In a statement to Fox News Digital, Purdue offered its condolences and said it would provide support to those affected. "We are saddened by this tragedy and the death of Julie and her family. We offer our condolences and support to her colleagues, peers, students and all who are affected," the university said. articles.title: Poland says Russia tried to assassinate Ukrainian rapper twice
articles.summary: Polish confirmation comes after Copenhagen reveals alleged Russian plot to kill US-Ukrainian citizen on Danish soil.
articles.body:
Polish authorities have said Russian intelligence services tried to kill a Ukrainian-American rapper visiting the country in August, after Copenhagen said Moscow had allegedly targeted the same man on Danish soil.

The alleged assassination plan targeted Albert Vasiliev, a rapper who performs under the name Kyivstoner and holds Ukrainian and US citizenship, according to Danish media.

Polish Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Maciej Wewior confirmed the alleged plot to kill Vasiliev in Poland to The Associated Press news agency on Sunday.

On Friday, in response to Denmark’s statement about the alleged assassination plan, Poland’s Foreign Ministry had written, “It is the second assassination attempt against the same person. The first one was foiled on the Polish territory in August 2026.”

It also said that a Russian national had been arrested.

Polish authorities detained the suspect, who was allegedly recruited by Moscow, on August 7.

Denmark announced the expulsion of a Russian diplomat on Friday after it accused Moscow intelligence of plotting the assassination during a concert in a Copenhagen suburb in September.

Denmark’s intelligence agency, PET, said on the same day that it suspected Russia of planning the assassination with the help of a banned Danish gang.

Two Danish men appeared ⁠in court near Copenhagen on Friday, charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service and attempted murder.

Russia dismissed the allegations through its embassy in Copenhagen, saying they were unsubstantiated.

Previously, on August 13, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk disclosed that a plot to kill a Ukrainian-American in Warsaw was thwarted. He did not disclose Vasiliev’s name at the time but said the target “was uncomfortable” for Russian President Vladimir Putin’s government.

Vasiliev has expressed his support for Ukraine amid Russia’s ongoing war on the country and was performing across Europe this year before his concerts were cancelled for security reasons.

Russia’s domestic security service, the FSB, accused Vasiliev of being involved in supplying drones for an alleged Ukrainian attack on a defence enterprise in the Moscow region. It said he was “acting under the patronage” of Ukraine’s internal security service, the SBU.

Danish broadcaster DR reported that Vasiliev denied the FSB accusations.

Danish Minister for Foreign Affairs Lars Lokke Rasmussen told reporters on Friday that Denmark was also considering suspending Schengen visas for Russians.

Poland’s Foreign Ministry said it backed the move.

“Poland supports measures Denmark suggested to limit the access and freedom of travel of Russian nationals on the EU territory,” it said on X.

Western officials have accused Russia and its proxies of staging dozens of attacks and other incidents across Europe since Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

articles.title: Seattle airport operator 'outraged' over ICE arrest of two passengers
articles.summary: ICE said a man and a woman, both Mexican nationals, were arrested for allegedly overstaying their visas.
articles.body:
US immigration authorities faced criticism after Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers arrested two passengers as they were boarding a flight in Seattle.

The incident happened on Saturday morning local time at the Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA), when ICE said a man and a woman, both Mexican nationals, were arrested for allegedly overstaying their visas.

It said that, during its arrest of the man - named as Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza - "other travellers began to obstruct and assault our law enforcement officers", which it described as a "federal crime and a felony".

The Port said in a statement that it was "outraged" about the incident.

Alaska Airlines said the incident happened during the boarding of one of its flights to Los Angeles and that it was not given "appropriate notice of the enforcement action".

It also said it was "concerned" about the arrests and recognised "how distressing this incident has been for employees and guests".

Both the airline and the Port of Seattle, which owns and runs the airport, said they were looking into whether the proper protocols were followed.

The Port said: "Immigration enforcement actions at SEA are conducted without the Port's participation or knowledge."

According to ICE, the woman they arrested - named as Sofia Hernandez Mejia - "hurled hot coffee on the officers" and would be charged with assaulting a federal officer.

Olia Catala, a lawyer for both Mendoza and Mejia - who are father and daughter - told local NBC affiliate King 5 News that they have "absolutely no criminal history".

"They're not fugitives. They're going through a legal process," Catala added.

The family has reportedly said that the ICE officers were in plain clothes and approached Mendoza and Mejia without identification.

"You can imagine if somebody's running at you who is not dressed as an officer, you don't know who they are," said Catala.

"So, there was a lot of panic, a lot of chaos, officers grabbing her, coffee spilling."

Video of the arrests taken by eyewitnesses appears to show two agents wearing masks, plain jackets and khaki trousers.

One eyewitness, John Gaedeke, who was also boarding the plane, told the Reuters news agency he thought the agents were passengers and that they "didn't have any identification".

Gaedeke said the agents "pointed and then they said now, and then they just lunged forward, didn't identify themselves" before "tackling" a man.

"Coffee definitely went flying, but to me, it looked like the passenger was holding it in their hand, and when they were tackled, it went everywhere. I didn't see anyone throw coffee," he added.

The Port of Seattle said it had "continually asked, and local federal immigration authorities have previously agreed to protocols at SEA, and we are in conversation with DHS [the Department of Homeland Security] on whether any of these protocols were breached".

According to the port's website, federal agents have access to airport property and port officials cannot interfere with operations. It says that the port has not historically been given advanced information about immigration enforcement, even when this takes place on its property.

Alaska Airlines said it is "required to comply with applicable laws and regulations when interacting with law enforcement officials".

"We do not direct or coordinate immigration enforcement activity, and we remain committed to protecting the privacy and safety of our guests and employees wherever possible," it added.

Washington's Democratic Governor Bob Ferguson told a press conference on Saturday that "ICE is completely out of control".

"We need a system of immigration enforcement, border security that is effective, ethical, and humane and ICE is not it. It is beyond reform."

Katie Garrow, the executive secretary of MLK Labor - which represents flight attendants, pilots and airport employees - said the incident had been "so upsetting and disturbing to workers" that four of the six crew on the flight chose not to fly.

Deportations of people found to be in the US illegally have ramped up significantly under Donald Trump's presidency but the tactics used by ICE have made many Americans grow uncomfortable, including many of those who supported stricter restrictions broadly.

Immigration raids have caused controversy in a number of US cities, including Minneapolis, Minnesota, where ICE agents killed Renee Good and Alex Pretti earlier this year.

Thousands of people were evacuated from a concert in Manchester on Sunday night after tear gas was believed to have been let off in the crowd.

The incident happened towards the end of US rapper Don Toliver's show at the Co-op Live arena at about 22:00.

Greater Manchester Police said no serious injuries were reported and those affected were treated by emergency services.

The force said a major incident had been declared "to ensure emergency services and partner agencies can work together quickly and effectively to coordinate a safe response".

Footage on social media showed emergency services converge on the 23,500-capacity arena, while some concertgoers were seen coughing as they streamed out of the venue.

Police said the substance let off was believed to be tear gas.

In a statement, the force said: "All attendees are currently being safely evacuated as a precaution. Those showing signs of being impacted are being supported by emergency services, with thankfully no serious injuries reported.

These are people with a perverted mindset. No one has any problem with the original phrasing. Previously, instead of 'Jai Shri Ram', the phrase used was 'Jai Siya Ram'—but these people have even removed the name of Mother Sita..." Rai said.His remarks came amid a war of words between Maurya and Samajwadi Party (SP) president Akhilesh Yadav over the BJP's slogan, 'Radhe Radhe, Kamal Khila De' (May the lotus bloom).On Sunday, Maurya took a swipe at the SP, saying its leaders had earlier felt uneasy hearing 'Jai Shri Ram' and were now troubled even by the chant of 'Radhe Radhe'.In a post on X, Maurya said, “SP leaders earlier felt uneasy hearing ‘Jai Shri Ram’. Now they are troubled even by ‘Radhe Radhe’.”“In Ayodhya, ‘Jai Shri Ram’ resonates, while in Braj people greet each other by saying ‘Radhe Radhe’,” he said.Asking Yadav to clarify his position, the deputy chief minister said, “Does this mean people in Uttar Pradesh will now have to seek his permission before taking the name of their deity?”Maurya accused the SP of indulging in appeasement politics and said both ‘Jai Shri Ram’ and ‘Radhe Radhe’ would continue to resonate in Uttar Pradesh. He also claimed that the party's hopes of returning to power in the 2027 Assembly elections would be dashed and that the BJP would form the government again.The exchange followed Yadav's remarks on Saturday, when he mocked the BJP's slogan during a press conference at the party headquarters in Lucknow.Referring to the slogan coined after the BJP's two-day meeting in Mathura, the former chief minister said the party was aware that its lotus symbol was wilting and was therefore chanting 'Radhe Radhe'.“‘Radhe Radhe’ is said at the time of farewell in our tradition. It means the BJP is going to be shown the door,” Yadav had said, claiming that the people of Uttar Pradesh would give the party a “grand farewell” in the coming elections.On Sunday, responding to Maurya's remarks, Yadav said, "I would never invite him to my house in my lifetime. But you (reporter) are welcome to visit our house; we will show you 'Radhe Radhe'.""'Radhe Radhe Kamal Khila De' go ahead and make it bloom. Does it mean the lotus has withered? Why do you (BJP) need to make it bloom again? It has withered," he said at a press conference.Yadav also accused the BJP of selectively invoking religious sentiments, clarifying that his party was not opposed to 'katha' (religious discourses) but objected to controversial remarks about Hindu deities."The Samajwadi Party is not against 'katha'. But what were the views expressed about the father of Lord Shri Ram and what was said about our Lord Krishna? These are the same BJP people who once made Lord Hanuman dance at their programme," he said without naming anyone."Can you make such remarks about Lord Ram's father? articles.title: ‘Extremely concerning’: Inside a US Army plan to detonate Iowa lead stores
articles.summary: Army plans to invoke emergency powers to detonate 4 tonnes of lead azide in an Iowa town, despite a court-ordered stay.
articles.body:
The United States Army intends to detonate more than 4 tonnes of lead azide at a military base in Iowa, defying a federal appeals court’s order suspending its permit to do so.

In a fact sheet this weekend, the Iowa Department of Health and Human Services said that two controlled explosions were scheduled for around noon (06:00 GMT) on Monday.

That announcement follows statements from the Department of Justice, arguing that Tuesday was the cut-off date to carry out a planned detonation.

Lead azide is a key explosive used in military ammunition. The Iowa stockpile has reportedly grown unstable, and Justice Department lawyers have warned that sub-freezing temperatures could trigger an uncontrolled explosion.

“The real choice, in other words, is not between a detonation and no detonation. It is between a planned and mitigated detonation and an unplanned and unmitigated explosion,” their court filing said.

But critics have questioned the army’s rationale for pushing ahead with the planned detonation, despite the court order to pause it.

“Anyone can claim an emergency at any point and do whatever they want. I don’t think people can or should accept that,” said Thien Chau, a lawyer with the legal group Earthjustice, which represents the plaintiffs in the lawsuit.

Chau told Al Jazeera that not enough has been done to mitigate the risk from the explosions, which are expected to release a cloud of lead into the air.

Experts say there is no safe level of lead exposure, and the dense metal can cause birth defects, brain damage and infertility.

“Anyone who hears that the army plans to explode nearly 10,000 pounds [4,500kg] of [this chemical] would recognise that that is not normal,” Chau said.

“That is extraordinary, and that is not something that you just take lightly.”

The impending explosions come after a tense legal battle between the US government and environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and the Iowa Environmental Council.

The groups have questioned the legality of an emergency permit the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) granted on November 13. The EPA authorised the Army to move forward with the explosions, originally scheduled for November 20.

The plaintiffs pointed out that nearby residents were only given a week’s notice and that the blasts could send lead dust as far as 160km (100 miles).

They also argued that the EPA failed to properly assess safer disposal methods.

The US Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit granted a pause on Friday. But in a Saturday court filing, the Justice Department maintained that the Army could still proceed with the two controlled blasts under an emergency exemption.

“The emergency exception does not depend on the Emergency Permit and is therefore not affected by, nor contradictory to, the terms of this Court’s administrative stay,” the Justice Department said in its filing.

But Earthjustice has argued that such a manoeuvre would sidestep the court’s authority.

Government lawyers have “laid the groundwork for a possible detonation without a permit, which would effectively bypass judicial process and review”, lawyer Rachel Rintelmann wrote in a Friday filing.

The controversy centres on a deteriorating stockpile of explosives stored for more than two decades at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant near the city of Middletown.

The stockpile contains roughly 9,700 pounds (4.4 tonnes) of lead azide across 68 barrels, with lead accounting for approximately 6,900 pounds (about 3.1 tonnes) of its chemical mass.

The explosives had been kept in a mixture of water and ethanol to ensure their stability. But in March, military technicians at the facility discovered that the system was breaking down.

According to a court declaration , an Army munitions expert found that the liquid in the drums had evaporated, causing needle-shaped crystals to form.

That recrystallisation puts the lead azide at risk of exploding on its own, as a result of temperature charges or even friction. So many crystals had formed that it was no longer safe to even open the barrels, according to the expert.

But on Sunday, Earthjustice released a statement questioning how this problem was allowed to develop in the first place.

“This emergency is of the Army’s own making,” the statement said. “The Army has not publicly provided details about why the lead azide was not disposed of before it became so dangerous. ”

The US Army has said the barrels are set to be detonated in place at the Iowa facility.

But it claims to have explored other options as well. According to the Army’s environmental assessment , it has previously considered two alternatives: chemically neutralising the explosives, or transporting them to an on-site detonation facility.

It rejected both ideas due to concerns that handling or transporting the explosives could trigger an accidental detonation.

Burying the drums, meanwhile, risked subjecting the shock-sensitive material to jolts that could similarly cause an unintended explosion.

What should residents do before and after the explosions?

But the health risks of even a planned explosion have put residents and environmental groups on edge.

On November 15, the Army released two plume maps outlining the potential spread of lead contamination across a swath of eastern Iowa, though projections hinge on real-time wind conditions.

The first map traces what could happen if a lead-bearing plume drifts northward, with a potential airborne trajectory over communities like Burlington, Muscatine, Davenport, Iowa City and Cedar Rapids.

The second map presents a more tenacious problem: surface exposure.

As the plume tracks north, heavier lead-bearing particles are expected to coat the landscape, landing on outdoor furniture, cars, soil and crops.

Residents in the projected plume path were advised to shelter indoors with their pets, shut windows, and limit exposure to outdoor air during a precautionary period, pending the Army’s all-clear.

Those living near Middletown City Park and Butterfly Park were also instructed to leave their homes for six hours to avoid ground vibrations that could crack or shatter nearby windows.

In the plume’s aftermath, the Army said residents would need to hose down outdoor surfaces, vehicles, and play equipment in an effort to flush away any lead dust deposited during the detonation.

But experts have expressed doubt about how practical the safety guidance is.

At a news briefing, University of Iowa professor David Cwiertny, the director of the Center for Health Effects of Environmental Contamination, warned that long-term monitoring would be necessary to track the lead’s distribution.

“We know that, unlike a porch or patio table, you cannot simply wipe down farm fields, gardens or topsoil because those surfaces are hard to clean,” Cwiertny said.

“We will ultimately need to rely on actual field samples after the event to measure how much lead settles there and understand what it means for our land, those crops and the quality of the environment.”

The Army has yet to issue revised instructions or specify new evacuation hours following the delayed detonation.

Earthjustice lawyers like Chau say the lack of communication is part of the problem.

“The way they’ve gone about notifying people and claiming that they’re going to clean things up when they don’t even know the extent of impact, that is extremely concerning,” Chau told Al Jazeera.

US Representative Eric Sorensen, the only meteorologist serving in Congress, said the Army should be looking at a window of opportunity that presents the least potential for off-site exposure.

In a video posted on Thursday, Sorensen said, “The most optimum conditions for controlled detonation would be when we have an inversion of clouds, warm air over cool, with light winds.”

He warned that the National Weather Service’s forecast does not offer those favourable conditions over the coming week, and he questioned why the detonations were only announced when cold weather was imminent.

Other questions remain about whether the Army has exhausted every practicable means of containing the lead’s spread.

Bruce Lanphear, a paediatric epidemiologist and professor of health sciences at Simon Fraser University, told Al Jazeera that it should be up to the Army to provide credible estimates of airborne lead concentrations, ground-level deposition and exposure levels before taking action.

“The burden should be on them to demonstrate that this is the least harmful option, not merely the fastest way to eliminate an immediate danger,” Lanphear told Al Jazeera.

articles.title: Lucknow woman, lover plot husband’s murder after catching him sexually abusing her daughter
articles.summary: Lucknow woman arrested for allegedly killing husband with paramour after catching him abusing her 6-year-old daughter; CCTV and mobile data helped police.
articles.body: LUCKNOW: A 35-year-old woman conspired with her paramour to murder her husband after catching him showing obscene videos to her six-year-old daughter and touching the child inappropriately, police said. The woman, Jyoti Kashyap, was arrested on Sunday evening, while her paramour Manoj Kumar remains on the run.The body of Jyoti’s husband Deepak Kashyap (40) was found near Lotus Portico Oro City in Jankipuram on Nov 17. Post-mortem confirmed murder, following which police registered a case on a complaint filed by the victim’s brother, Ramu Kashyap, against Jyoti and others.DCP, North Zone, Amit Kumar Anand, said Jyoti told investigators she had caught Deepak allegedly showing obscene videos to her daughter and touching her inappropriately around 15 days before the murder. She claimed the incident prompted her to confide in Manoj, with whom she had grown close over the past year.Jyoti also alleged that Deepak would assault her after consuming alcohol, force her to drink and pressure her into performing unnatural sex.Jyoti married Deepak, a native of Mahmoodabad in Sitapur, in 2023. It was her third marriage, while Deepak had also married twice earlier. Jyoti has a six-year-old daughter from her previous marriage, while Deepak had three children from his first marriage.The couple initially lived with Jyoti’s parents in Gudamba before taking up jobs at a private school in Aliganj around one and a half years ago. Deepak worked as a driver, while Jyoti was employed as an attendant. They later rented a room near the school.Police said Manoj, a friend of Deepak, had grown close to Jyoti after Deepak introduced him to the family. Jyoti confided in him about her marital problems and discussed separation, but feared social stigma over her third marriage.According to police, the two subsequently plotted to kill Deepak. On the night of Nov 16, Jyoti told her drunk husband she was unwell and needed to visit a doctor before calling Manoj, who arrived on his motorcycle.The trio reached near Oro City, where Jyoti got off on the pretext of nausea. While Deepak and Manoj were talking, she allegedly struck Deepak on the head with a brick from behind. The duo then stuffed cloth into his mouth and strangled him before fleeing.The murder was unravelled through CCTV footage, mobile surveillance and other technical evidence. A joint team of Jankipuram police, SWAT and surveillance personnel arrested Jyoti near Chhuiyapurwa liquor shop. articles.title: US intelligence chief defends Trump’s comments calling Putin his ‘friend’
articles.summary: US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton says Trump’s comments were ‘entirely appropriate’ in context of summit.
articles.body:
United States Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton has faced pressure to justify President Donald Trump’s claims that his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin is a “friend”.

In an appearance on the ABC News show This Week, journalist Jonathan Karl pressed Clayton on Trump’s recent remarks.

“Is Vladimir Putin America’s friend? Because Trump said he couldn’t answer that question,” Karl asked.

Clayton responded by calling Trump’s meeting “historic” and his remarks “appropriate”, but the intelligence chief also clarified that the US has not taken Russia’s side when it comes to the country’s invasion of Ukraine.

“Is Vladimir Putin America’s friend? He is not America’s friend in Ukraine. Not at all. Not at all,” Clayton said.

The scrutiny follows a first-ever confirmed meeting between Trump, Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping on November 19.

The three world leaders had a roundtable on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) conference in Shenzhen, China.

Throughout his presidency, Trump has repeatedly praised Putin. In August 2025, Trump hosted the Russian leader in Alaska for Putin’s first visit to the US in nearly a decade.

Upon reuniting with Putin at the Shenzhen conference, Trump offered him a warm, light-hearted greeting.

“Who is he?” Trump joked, first pointing to Putin, then striding across the room to shake his hand. “He’s my friend.”

Trump has since doubled down on his remarks, posting several images of their meeting on social media, one of which bore the caption , “My Friend”.

When a reporter asked whether Russia was a “friend to America” in a news briefing on Friday, Trump brushed aside the question.

“I can’t speak to America,” Trump said, proceeding to explain that he and Putin had grown close during an investigation into whether Russia had interfered in his favour during the 2016 US presidential election.

“I’ve been dealing with Putin during the fake Russia, Russia, Russia hoax. And to be honest, he was very nice about it,” Trump explained.

The US State Department has long been critical of Russia over allegations of human rights abuses, including the torture and imprisonment of political dissidents.

Washington has also supported Ukraine after Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, providing billions in security assistance and weaponry.

Under Trump, however, that support has cooled, with the US president openly criticising his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, for failing to cut a deal with Russia.

Such remarks have divided Republicans, with critics like outgoing US Representative Don Bacon accusing Trump of “playing footsie” with Putin.

“Traditionally, Republicans stood up to Russia and China,” Bacon said last week. “We stood for freedom, and we stood up for countries that shared our values. President Trump has been terrible on this, right here.”

But in his television appearances on Sunday, Clayton defended Trump’s remarks, describing the president’s statements of friendship as “entirely appropriate” for building a personal rapport with the Russian leader.

He also praised Trump for uniting some of the world’s biggest powers for a conversation about nuclear proliferation.

“It should be assuring that you have the three world nuclear powers getting together and saying: We’re not going to go in that direction,” Clayton told This Week.

While the trilateral meeting concluded with a statement about “reducing nuclear risks”, critics point out no firm commitments were made.

Also on Sunday, in an appearance on CNN, Clayton reiterated his support for Trump’s remarks.

“In that context, whatever language the president wants to use, I trust him completely,” Clayton said.

articles.title: Man convicted for role in Tessa Majors' 2019 NYC killing released on parole
articles.summary: Luchiano Lewis, convicted in the 2019 murder of Barnard College freshman Tessa Majors, was freed on conditional parole after serving fewer than seven years behind bars.
articles.body: One of the three then-teenagers convicted in connection with the 2019 murder of Barnard College freshman Tessa Majors in New York City has now been released on conditional parole supervision, according to the New York State Department of Corrections and Community Supervision. Luchiano Lewis, now 21, was released on Oct. 14 under conditional release and placed under community supervision after serving fewer than seven years behind bars for his role in the robbery and killing in Manhattan's Morningside Park in December 2019, state correction records show. Lewis, who was released from the Franklin Correctional Facility, had been sentenced to nine years to life after pleading guilty in 2021 to second-degree murder and first-degree robbery in connection with Majors' killing. MARYLAND MAN ACCUSED OF GIRL'S FATAL SHOOTING RELEASED FROM PRISON DAYS BEFORE Under New York State law, Lewis' conditional release did not require him to go before the State Board of Parole because eligible inmates can qualify for conditional release after serving two-thirds of their minimum sentence, subject to applicable requirements and good-time allowances. Majors, who was 18 when she was killed, was attacked on Dec. 11, 2019, near a staircase in Morningside Park. Prosecutors said a group of teens confronted Majors in an attempted robbery, during which she was stabbed multiple times. She was eventually able to climb a set of stairs and reach the street before collapsing. She was taken to a hospital, where she died from her injuries. JUDGE SENTENCES LILY PETERS' KILLER 4 YEARS AFTER 10-YEAR-OLD FOUND DEAD IN WOODS After the crime, then-14-year-old Lewis and another 14-year-old were both tried as adults for the attack. Prosecutors said Lewis held Majors in a headlock while the other 14-year-old stabbed her multiple times. While Lewis was not holding the knife in the attack, prosecutors said he played a key role in the robbery that killed Majors. At Lewis' sentencing, Manhattan Supreme Court Justice Robert Mandelbaum said the killing "tore at the fabric of the entire city." "The defendant was and is extremely young. He has his whole life ahead of him, but Tessa Majors does not," he added. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Majors' parents described the lasting impact of the loss of their child during Lewis' sentencing, remembering her as a talented student, musician and writer whose future was tragically ended too soon. The two other teenagers convicted in connection with the killing — Rashaun Weaver, who was 14 at the time of the crime, and Zyairr Davis, who was 13 at the time — remain behind bars. Weaver was sentenced to 14 years to life in prison for murder and robbery, while Davis pleaded guilty to robbery and was sentenced to 18 months in juvenile detention. Davis completed his juvenile sentence but is now being held on an unrelated attempted murder case.

articles.title: Indonesian police remove 24 body bags from factory fire site
articles.summary: Authorities in Java are searching for dozens of missing workers as they continue to battle remaining hotspots.
articles.body:
Indonesian authorities are set to resume the search for missing workers on Monday after police removed 24 body bags from a factory in Java gutted by a fire.

Firefighters continued to battle remaining hotspots on Sunday after the blaze broke out on Saturday evening at the PT Fonusa Agung Mulia candy factory in Cikande, Serang regency, West Java province.

A search for dozens of missing workers was suspended overnight but would resume Monday morning, Hendra Kurniawan, the police chief of Indonesia’s Banten province, told local broadcaster Metro TV on Sunday.

Steven Erwin Wijaya, the CEO of the factory’s parent company, PT United Family Food, said at a news conference that about 300 people were present for Saturday’s shift, with 65 of them believed to have been in the affected area when the fire broke out.

In a statement that followed, the factory said 24 of the 65 workers had returned home, four were receiving medical treatment, 29 remained ‌missing, and the whereabouts of another eight had yet to be confirmed.

At a news conference on Sunday, Wahyu Hidayati Dwi Palupi, a police disaster victim identification official, said the intensity of the fire had made it impossible to identify the recovered victims visually. She said they would collect DNA samples from relatives and the personal belongings of the missing workers, a process that could take two to three weeks.

Photos and videos circulating online on Sunday showed flames and thick smoke coming from the factory, which borders the capital, Jakarta. Footage from inside the three-storey building appeared to show the fire caused extensive damage, with equipment blackened and destroyed.

Indonesia has suffered several deadly fires in recent years.

A fire in an office building in Jakarta killed at least 22 people last December. An explosion at an Indonesian nickel-processing plant killed at least 13 people in 2023.
